rules.title: Ban on using or distributing a common pricing algorithm as part of a conspiracy to restrain trade
rules.requirement: Under California antitrust law (Cartwright Act), it is illegal to use or distribute a shared pricing algorithm, such as rent-setting software that uses competitor data, as part of an agreement or conspiracy to restrain trade. If you suspect landlords are coordinating rents through such software, you can report it to the Attorney General.

rules.quoted_span: (a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.

coverage_conditions.summary: Applies statewide to any person (including landlords and software vendors) who uses or distributes a common pricing algorithm; not limited to particular buildings. End consumers are excluded from the definition of person.

rules.exemptions: "Person" does not include the end consumer of a product or service.
rules.penalty: Violation of the Cartwright Act, which is punishable as a crime; general Cartwright Act enforcement applies.

rules.title: Application screening fee cap
rules.requirement: A landlord may charge an application screening fee no higher than the actual out-of-pocket cost of screening you, and never more than $30 per applicant, adjusted annually for CPI increases since 1998. Ask for the current CPI-adjusted figure if you are charged more than $30. A landlord may not charge you a screening fee if they know or should know that no unit is available now or within a reasonable time. A landlord may charge a screening fee only if they either consider complete applications in order received under written criteria (approving the first qualified applicant and charging only when your application is actually considered, refunding within 7 days if collected by mistake), or refund the full fee to every applicant not selected within 7 days of selection or 30 days of application, whichever is first. The landlord must give you an itemized receipt (in person, by mail, or by email if agreed) showing out-of-pocket costs and time spent, and must return any part of the fee not used if no reference check or credit report was obtained. If you paid a screening fee, the landlord must give you a copy of your consumer credit report within seven days of receiving it, by personal delivery, mail, or email.
rules.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant. The thirty dollar ($30) application screening fee may be adjusted annually by the landlord or their agent commensurate with an increase in the Consumer Price Index, beginning on January 1, 1998.

rules.title: Tenant Protection Act just-cause eviction requirement
rules.requirement: Once all tenants have lawfully lived in the unit for 12 months (or at least one tenant for 24 months), your landlord may evict only for a listed at-fault or no-fault just cause, and the cause must be stated in the written termination notice. For a curable lease violation, the landlord must first give you a notice and a chance to fix it. If your landlord ends a covered tenancy for a no-fault reason (owner move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order, or demolition or substantial remodel), they must either pay you one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 calendar days of the notice or waive your final month's rent in writing. The notice must tell you about this right; if the landlord does not strictly comply, the notice is void.

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act statewide rent cap
rules.requirement: For a covered unit, your landlord cannot raise your rent by more than 5% plus local CPI, or 10%, whichever is lower, in any 12-month period, measured from the lowest rent charged in the prior 12 months. rules.title: Source-of-income discrimination ban in housing
rules.requirement: A landlord may not refuse to rent to you, harass you, or treat you differently because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8 vouchers, VASH vouchers and other public assistance or housing subsidies. Rental ads also may not state a preference against such income sources. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord's minimum-income requirement must be based only on the part of the rent you pay, not the full rent. If you have a government rent subsidy, a landlord who uses credit history must let you instead provide other verifiable proof you can pay your share of rent (such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements), give you reasonable time to provide it, and reasonably consider it in place of your credit history.

rules.title: Security deposit cap of one month's rent
rules.requirement: Your landlord cannot demand or take a security deposit of more than one month's rent, on top of first month's rent. A small landlord (a natural person or an LLC of natural persons owning no more than two rental properties with no more than four units in total) may charge up to two months' rent, but not to a service member. If you are a service member and are charged a higher-than-standard deposit due to credit or housing history, the landlord must give you a written explanation by lease signing and return the extra amount after no more than six months if you are not behind on rent. Within 21 days after you move out, your landlord must return your deposit and give an itemized statement of deductions, with receipts and photos for repair or cleaning charges. Deductions cannot cover ordinary wear and tear, and bad-faith retention can cost the landlord up to twice the deposit plus actual damages. A lease cannot call any deposit or upfront security charge "nonrefundable"; such a clause is not allowed.
